# 5 Practical Strategies for Practicing DSA Problems

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/Der3XLgjh4R/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** level5esper · **Saved:** 2026-10-20

## Summary

Tackling challenging data structures and algorithms problems effectively requires systematic problem-solving strategies rather than immediately looking at solutions. Working out small examples by hand, checking constraints to infer time complexity, stress testing against a brute-force implementation, upsolving missed problems, and allowing ideas time to marinate help build lasting algorithmic intuition.

## Caption

Here are 5 concrete ways to practice your next DSA problem when you're stuck. Most people skip the last one.

Each of these gets you to find the next idea in the problem yourself, before you look at anyone's solution. A small case gives you something to check an idea against. The constraints cut down what can even work. The USACO Guide's table says n up to 20 allows O(2ⁿ·n), and n up to 5·10⁵ needs about O(n log n). A brute force gives you correct answers to check your fast code against. The Kadane bug in the video starts best at 0, which only fails when every number is negative, like [-2, -3]. Hand-picked tests miss it, and random small tests catch it almost right away. Upsolving and mind solving both give you another go at the ideas you missed. AtCoder posts an official editorial for each Beginner Contest problem. When you upsolve one, read only until you see what you didn't notice, then finish it yourself.

Send this to a friend who's stuck on DSA, and follow me for more DSA tips.
